description.fr: Version du copilote John B. Whitted, en place droite — le côté par lequel l'objet est passé, et le seul des deux à avoir vu la fin. Vue depuis le poste de pilotage du DC-3 à 1500 m — d'où le sol, très bas, et le ciel de nuit du 24 juillet 1948. Il voit l'arrivée de face, le passage à droite, la ressource abrupte, puis la phase finale que Chiles n'a pas vue : une ascension verticale courte et très rapide (ici ~14° d'arc en 1,2 s, de l'ordre des 1300 km/h estimés au sol depuis Robins) au terme de laquelle l'objet disparaît instantanément. Cette disparition est déclarée telle quelle et non « dans un nuage » : interrogé par McDonald en 1968, Whitted a explicitement démenti cette lecture des premiers interrogatoires. Distance : les deux hommes n'ont jamais pu s'accorder (l'un sous 1000 ft, l'autre plusieurs fois cela), et McDonald ne dit pas lequel disait quoi. L'enregistrement ne tranche pas, et ne le peut pas : il ne déclare que des tailles angulaires, et une distance ne s'en déduit que là où l'objet croise un élément de décor dont la position est connue — ce qu'un ciel de nuit vide n'offre nulle part. Le dessin suit le cadrage du relevé officiel (~180 m au plus près), qui reste donc un choix de mise en scène et non une affirmation du fichier. Le compte rendu est désormais joué en 3D, et c'est là, et seulement là, qu'une distance est affirmée : le corps est le cylindre à bouts francs de son propre dessin, long de 30 m et épais de 5,40, avec ses deux rangées de trois hublots et son dessous noir, et c'est cette épaisseur — la seule mesure du dessin qui ne dépende pas de l'angle sous lequel on le voit — qui donne la portée, 701 m à l'arrivée, 183 m au plus près et 935 m au dernier instant où il le voit encore. La largeur dit de combien il s'était tourné, et le cap qui en découle tient à quinze degrés près tout du long. Il ne cabre pas pendant la ressource, parce qu'il n'a rien dessiné de tel — et c'est ce qui fait qu'à la fin, presque à la verticale au-dessus d'eux, le corps couvre deux fois la hauteur de sa dernière boîte : un désaccord que le lecteur affiche au lieu de le corriger. Forme d'après le dessin que Whitted lui-même a remis au projet Sign (Blue Book, rapport n° 14, cas 5) : un cylindre nettement plus épais, à bouts francs, portant deux rangées de trois ouvertures qu'il annote « fenêtres avec lumière blanche » au-dessus d'un dessous « noir » — là où Chiles n'a dessiné aucun hublot. La flamme fait 40 pieds pour 100 de fuselage, les deux chiffres étant de sa main sur ce même dessin (« ORANGE & RED FLAME 40' LONG », « 100' LENGTH ») — et non les 50 pieds que reprennent les commentateurs ultérieurs. Longueur rapportée ~30 m. Le virage d'évitement n'est pas reproduit : le format ne sait pas encore incliner le point de vue (roulis). L'appareil AVANCE, ce qu'un fichier qui répétait la même latitude à chaque keyframe ne disait pas : sa route porte le cap que le compte rendu donne au premier instant — l'objet arrive de face, donc ils regardent devant eux — et sa vitesse est la croisière ordinaire d'un DC-3, 288 km/h, soit 800 m de sol en dix secondes. Les deux sont ASSUMÉS : aucune source ne donne le cap ni la vitesse-sol de ce vol-là. Ce qui n'est pas assumé, c'est qu'un avion de ligne à 1500 m ne fait pas du surplace.
description.en: First officer John B. Whitted's account, in the right-hand seat — the side the object passed on, and the only one of the two to have seen the end. Seen from the DC-3's cockpit at 1,500 m — hence the very low ground, and the night sky of 24 July 1948. He sees it come head-on, pass to the right, the abrupt pull-up, then the final phase Chiles did not see: a short, very fast vertical climb (here ~14° of arc in 1.2 s, of the order of the 1,300 km/h estimated on the ground from Robins) at the end of which the object vanishes instantly. That disappearance is stated as such and not as “into a cloud”: questioned by McDonald in 1968, Whitted explicitly denied that reading of the early interviews. Distance: the two men could never agree (one under 1,000 ft, the other several times that), and McDonald does not say which said which. The recording does not settle it, and cannot: it states angular sizes only, and a distance follows from them just where the object crosses a piece of decor whose position is known — which an empty night sky offers nowhere. The drawing follows the official report's framing (~180 m at closest), which is therefore a staging choice and not a claim of the file. The account is now played in 3D, and that is where, and only where, a distance is claimed: the body is the blunt-ended cylinder of his own drawing, 30 m long and 5.40 thick, with its two rows of three windows and its black underside, and it is that thickness — the one measurement of the drawing that does not depend on which way it was seen — that gives the range: 701 m as it comes on, 183 m at its nearest, 935 m at the last instant he still has it. The width says how far round it had turned, and the heading that follows holds to within fifteen degrees throughout. It does not raise its nose through the pull-up, because he drew nothing of the kind — which is why at the end, nearly overhead, the body covers twice the height of his last box: a disagreement the reader shows rather than corrects. Shape after the drawing Whitted himself gave Project Sign (Blue Book, report no. 14, case 5): a distinctly thicker cylinder with blunt ends, carrying two rows of three openings he annotates “windows with white light” above an underside marked “black” — where Chiles drew no porthole at all. The flame is 40 feet to 100 of fuselage, both figures in his own hand on that same drawing (“ORANGE & RED FLAME 40' LONG”, “100' LENGTH”) — and not the 50 feet later commentators repeat. Reported length ~30 m. The avoidance bank is not reproduced: the format cannot yet roll the point of view. The aircraft MOVES, which a file repeating the same latitude at every keyframe did not say: its course is the heading the account gives at the first instant — the object comes head-on, so they are looking straight ahead — and its speed is a DC-3's ordinary cruise, 288 km/h, or 800 m of ground in ten seconds. Both are ASSUMED: no source gives that flight's course or ground speed. What is not assumed is that an airliner at 1,500 m does not hover.

title.fr: Le cylindre à deux rangées de hublots que Whitted a dessiné, à trente mètres de long
title.en: The cylinder with two rows of windows Whitted drew, thirty metres long

luminanceCdM2.rationale: Neither man gave a brightness. What they gave is a colour, and that is what sets this: against the sky of 02:45 and an eye adapted to it, the scene shows their deep blue only while the hull stays under about a quarter of a candela per square metre, and washes it to a white neither of them described above that. Two is the luminance of the brightest thing the model says glows — the windows he annotated "windows with white light" — and the fuselage burns at an eighth of it, which is the ratio the model carries, so the fuselage sits just under that edge. It is a small figure for a lit window, some hundred-and-twentieth of a fluorescent tube's, and it is chosen for the colour it reproduces and not from anything measured: it is the colour, not the number, that is the account. It was twelve while the scene showed the eye's response as a luminance on the screen; shown as a lightness since (see EYE_RESPONSE_GLSL), the same colour needs a sixth of the light, and a hull left at twelve came out a vivid blue no night shows.

Nobody measured it, and only Whitted put a figure on the flame at all, its length. What both men describe is a jet of orange and red seen against a moonless night from a few hundred metres, bright enough that they took it at first for the exhaust of a jet fighter: 120 000 cd/m² is the order of a rocket motor's plume and a tenth of the Socorro flame's assumed brightness, which was chosen against daylight and would be absurd here. What makes it right or wrong is the eye, not the account: the recording states a luminance so that the scene's own photometry decides how it reads at 02:45, and a better figure replaces this one without anything else changing.

track.rationale: Thirty metres long is the account's own figure, and Whitted wrote "100' LENGTH" on his drawing beside the 40 feet of flame. The distance is not: the two men never agreed on it, one under a thousand feet and the other several times that, and McDonald does not say which said which. Both are DERIVED here from the drawing itself, and nothing is derived from the length, which the drawing foreshortens. What it does not foreshorten is the THICKNESS: a body of revolution is its own diameter across the short way from any angle, so the 5.4 m the recording makes of the box's height fixes the range at every instant, 701 m as it comes on and 183 m at its nearest. That the nearest lands on the official report's own framing is not a confirmation: the drawing was laid out to it. The box's WIDTH then says how far round it had turned, 18° off end-on at the first instant and broadside by the last, and the heading that follows from that comes out at 180° on average and never more than fifteen degrees from it: Whitted's boxes, which say nothing about a course, are those of a thing holding one straight course while the aeroplane crossed it. Where it points UP is nowhere: through the pull-up it climbs without raising its nose, because his boxes stay as thin there as anywhere, and a thirty-metre body pitched thirty degrees is five times deeper on the glass than one flying level. Tilting it would manufacture a disagreement he never stated.
